title: Eating in… and out
summary: Talk about habits and things happening now. Learn food and cooking words.

blocks.p: Use the present simple for things that are always or generally true, and for things that happen regularly. Add -s / -es with he, she and it. Use do / does to make questions and negatives.
ex: I usually have toast and coffee in the morning.
My brother doesn't eat meat.
How often do you eat out?

blocks.p: Words like always, usually, often, sometimes, hardly ever, never go before the main verb but after the verb be. Longer expressions like every day or twice a week usually go at the end.
ex: She never cooks on Mondays.
I'm always hungry in the evening.
We get a takeaway every Friday.

blocks.h: Present continuous: now and around now
blocks.p: Use the present continuous (am / is / are + verb-ing) for actions in progress at the moment of speaking, or temporary situations around now.
ex: Can I call you back? I'm cooking dinner.
The price of olive oil is rising at the moment.
Is your sister still working at that café?
What time does the restaurant open?
Where are you having lunch today?

blocks.p: Some verbs describe states, feelings, opinions or the senses, not actions. We don't normally use them in the continuous form, even when we mean 'now'. Common ones: be, believe, belong, depend, hate, know, like, love, mean, need, prefer, realize, remember, seem, want, and the senses look, smell, taste, sound.
ex: I need a coffee right now.
This soup tastes amazing.
Do you know this restaurant?

blocks.p: A few verbs can be actions or states, with a different meaning. have: have lunch (action) vs. have a car (possession). think: think about something (action) vs. think that… (opinion).
ex: Sorry, I'm having a shower. I'll call you later.
My parents have a small flat by the sea.
What are you thinking about?
I think this café makes the best coffee in town.

blocks.p: English has short and long versions of some vowels. The long ones have the symbol ː. Making the vowel the right length can change the word.
ex: ship, sheep
full, fool
cod, cord

grammar.q: Can I call you back? I ___ dinner.
grammar.e: An action in progress now → present continuous.

grammar.q: My parents ___ out every Friday night.
grammar.e: A regular habit with a frequency expression → present simple.

grammar.q: This soup ___ delicious!
grammar.e: taste (= have a flavour) is a non-action verb: no continuous form.

grammar.q: I ___ a new phone. Mine is broken.
grammar.e: need is a non-action verb.

grammar.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: She is never late for work.
She never is late for work.
She is late never for work.
grammar.e: Adverbs of frequency go after the verb be.

grammar.q: Which sentence is correct?
grammar.e: have = possession is a state, so no continuous.

grammar.q: A: What ___ about? B: My holiday next month.
grammar.e: think about = an action happening now.

grammar.q: My sister ___ (not like) spicy food.
grammar.e: Third person negative: doesn't + infinitive.

grammar.q: Which question is correct?
o: What time does the shop open?
What time does open the shop?
grammar.e: QUASI: What time + does + the shop + open?

grammar.q: Be quiet! The baby ___ (sleep).
grammar.e: Happening now → present continuous.

grammar.q: I ___ (not believe) a word of his story!
grammar.e: believe is a non-action verb.

grammar.q: Where should 'usually' go? 'I ___ have ___ toast ___ for breakfast.'
o: I usually have toast for breakfast.
I have usually toast for breakfast.
I have toast usually for breakfast.
grammar.e: Before the main verb.

vocabulary.q: Meat from a young sheep is…
vocabulary.e: lamb = young sheep. Pork comes from pigs, beef from cows.

vocabulary.q: Vegetables cooked over boiling water are…
My doctor told me to ___ sugar completely.
vocabulary.e: cut out = stop completely; cut down on = have less.

vocabulary.q: I'm trying to ___ coffee. Only one cup a day now.
We don't cook much. We ___ ___ three times a week. (two words)
vocabulary.e: eat out = eat in a restaurant.

vocabulary.q: Potatoes cooked in the oven with a little oil are…

pronunciation.e: food /fuːd/. Cook and sugar have short /ʊ/.

pronunciation.q: Which word has a different vowel sound?
pronunciation.e: hot has short /ɒ/; pork and sauce have /ɔː/.

title: Modern families
summary: Talk about the future in three ways. Describe family members and personalities.

sections.title: Future forms: going to, present continuous, will / won't

blocks.h: be going to: plans and evidence
blocks.p: Use be going to + infinitive for things you have already decided to do, and for predictions when you can see evidence now.
ex: I'm going to learn to cook Thai food this year.
Look at the traffic! We're going to be late.
We aren't going to travel abroad this summer.

blocks.p: Use the present continuous for future arrangements: plans with a time, a place, other people, a ticket or a booking. It's very common with travel verbs: go, come, leave, arrive.
ex: My cousins are coming to stay next weekend.
I'm meeting my lawyer at ten tomorrow.
Dad is flying to Madrid on Monday and coming home on Thursday.

blocks.h: will / won't: instant decisions, promises, offers, predictions
blocks.p: Use will / won't when you decide at the moment of speaking, and for promises, offers and predictions (often with I think…).
ex: Someone's at the door. I'll open it.
I'll pay you back tomorrow. I promise.
I think you'll enjoy this book.

blocks.p: Use Shall I…? to offer help and Shall we…? to make suggestions.
ex: Shall I carry those bags for you?
Shall we order a pizza tonight?

groups.note: un-, dis- and in- make opposites. in- becomes im- before b, m, p; ir- before r; il- before l.

blocks.p: In words with two or more syllables, one syllable is stronger. Dictionaries mark it with ˈ before the stressed syllable. Prefixes like un- and in- are not usually stressed.
ex: ambitious /æmˈbɪʃəs/
reliable /rɪˈlaɪəbl/
competitive /kəmˈpetətɪv/
sociable /ˈsəʊʃəbl/

blocks.p: We stress the words that carry the meaning (nouns, main verbs, adjectives) and say small words like to, a, are, will quickly and weakly.
ex: We're going to have a party.
I'll call you tomorrow.

grammar.q: A: The phone's ringing. B: I ___ it.
grammar.e: Instant decision → will.

grammar.q: Look at that man on the ladder! He ___ fall.
grammar.e: Prediction with evidence you can see → going to.

grammar.q: We ___ dinner with the Smiths on Saturday. We've booked a table.
grammar.e: Fixed arrangement → present continuous.

grammar.q: ___ I open the window? It's hot in here.
grammar.e: Offer → Shall I…?

grammar.q: Don't worry. I ___ forget your birthday this year. I promise!
grammar.e: Promise → won't.

grammar.q: My cousin ___ study medicine. She decided last year.
grammar.e: A plan already decided → going to.

grammar.q: I think it ___ be sunny tomorrow.
grammar.e: Opinion-based prediction → will.

grammar.q: Their flight ___ (arrive) at 6.30 tomorrow morning. Use the present continuous.
grammar.e: Travel arrangement.

grammar.q: It's Mum's birthday tomorrow. I know! I ___ (make) her a cake. (instant decision)
grammar.e: Decision at the moment of speaking.

grammar.q: I've decided. I ___ (not / go) to the party. Use be going to.
grammar.e: A decision already made → be going to.

title: Practical English 1: Reacting to what people say
summary: Show interest and emotion when someone tells you news.

blocks.p: In conversation, good listeners react. Choose the phrase that matches the news.
table: You're kidding! / No way! / You're joking!
That's great news! / How fantastic! / Congratulations!
Oh no! / I'm so sorry. / What a pity! / How awful!

blocks.p: Two useful patterns: How + adjective! and What (a) + noun! Use a / an with singular countable nouns.
ex: How amazing!
How awful!
What a pity!
What a good idea!
What terrible news!

blocks.p: Sound interested: your voice should go up and down a lot. A flat voice sounds bored or rude.
ex: Really? That's great news!
Oh no! I'm so sorry.
